title: Mara's generals
hookLine: in one of the oldest tellings, Mara's army has no elephants: it's desire, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth, fear and doubt

lines: THE KIND VOICE: TAKE A BREAK.
cards: Some voices that stop you aren't angry at all. They're kind. You're worn out, one says.
Take a break. You've done enough. Why push so hard when you could be doing something nice and useful instead?

On day fifty-two you met Mara, the tempter, with his later, enormous army of elephants and storms. The Padhana Sutta, the discourse on striving, may be one of the oldest poems about Mara and the wanderer.
And here, Mara opens with sympathy.

teach.h: THE KIND VOICE: LIVE, WHY STRUGGLE?
teach.b: By the Neranjara river, the wanderer is striving hard, thin from fasting. Mara, here called Namuci, comes with gentle words. You're thin and pale; death is close.
Live, sir! Living, you could do good deeds and earn merit. Why struggle?
The answer is firm. I don't need merit. I have faith, energy, wisdom.
As my body wastes, my mind grows clearer. Then he names the army, rank by rank.
Desire is your first army. The second, discontent. The third, hunger and thirst.
The fifth, sloth and drowsiness. The sixth, fear. The seventh, doubt.
The eighth, contempt and stubbornness. Then gain, fame, honor, a reputation wrongly won, praising yourself and looking down on others. This, Namuci, is your army.
Notice who the generals are. Not demons from outside. Every one of them can turn up inside an ordinary person on a slow afternoon.
Even fame and praise are in the ranks. Then the line the poem turns on.
On the old Indian battlefield, the commentary says, a soldier who would never retreat tied on a tuft of munja grass as a sign. Should I wear the munja grass? Shame on a life lived defeated.

Better for me to die in battle than to live beaten. At the poem's end, Mara says he followed the Buddha for seven years and never found an opening. He's like a crow pecking at a stone that looked like fat.
He drops his lute and disappears.

how: Buddhist teachers often use the list of Mara's armies to help meditators recognize hindrances as they arise, and Mara's defeat is a common subject of temple murals.

o: the monks who guarded the Buddha at night
kings who fought wars against the Sakyans
inner forces like doubt and fear that stop you

games.q: Mara's armies, in order: tap the pairs.

s: in the Padhana Sutta, Mara first comes with gentle, sympathetic words
you're thin, death is close, live and do good deeds instead.
this early poem describes Mara riding an elephant with storms
that's the later telling; here his army is desire, discontent, fear, doubt and the rest.
fame and honor are listed among Mara's forces
gain, fame, honor and ill-won reputation join the ranks.

games.q: you're exhausted by the river. a gentle voice says: you'll die like this. live, do good deeds, why struggle? what does the wanderer say?
o: you're right; I'll rest and go home.
I have faith, energy and wisdom; better to die fighting than live defeated.
games.why: he names Mara's armies one by one and says it's better to die in battle than to live defeated.

practice: Sit, and if one of Mara's generals shows up, discontent, drowsiness, doubt, a craving for your phone, don't fight it with force. Just name it quietly by rank: ah, the fifth army, or there's doubt.
Naming takes away its disguise; then come back to the breath and stay, and that staying is the munja grass.

wordCard.voice: Mara's generals. In the Padhana Sutta: desire, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth, fear, doubt, contempt and the pull of fame, an army that lives inside.

orig.note: Pali padhana: striving, exertion. the name of Sn 3.2.

carryVoice: Your line: better to fight than yield. The kind, tired voice has a name, and a rank. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Commentary on Sn 3.2: the munja grass as a sign of no retreat
